summaries.example: Imagine a stream that starts with 0 and then has itself as its tail: 0, 0, 0, 0, and so on. We can describe it as a looping object, or we can describe its unfolded pattern as an endless list of zeros. The entry asks whether these should count as the same mathematical thing and how set theory can represent them.
summaries.summary: Non-wellfounded set theory studies mathematical objects with circular structure. A set might contain itself, or objects might form an endless membership chain. Standard set theory rules this out with the Foundation Axiom. The entry examines an alternative, the Anti-Foundation Axiom, which says that every suitable graph—a collection of points joined by arrows—has one unique way to turn its points into sets. This lets mathematicians model looping streams, infinitely deep trees, and other circular patterns. The entry also compares two ways of describing things: building them from simpler parts step by step, and understanding them through their repeating structure. Streams show the idea clearly. A stream has a head and a tail, and its tail may be the stream itself. It can also be unfolded into an endless sequence. The entry asks whether these descriptions are merely different ways to talk about one object or whether the difference matters. It connects these ideas with coalgebra, a mathematical approach that studies systems by their transitions and observations.
key_ideas: Some kinds of circularity cause trouble, but others can be useful or harmless.
A stream can be pictured as a head followed by another stream, even when the tail eventually returns to the starting stream.
Standard set theory uses the Foundation Axiom, while non-wellfounded set theory studies what happens when it is replaced by the Anti-Foundation Axiom.
Graphs, streams, and trees can be used as pictures for sets and other mathematical objects.
The same object may have different descriptions, such as a looping stream and an endless list.
summaries.why_it_matters: Circular patterns appear in many kinds of mathematics and in descriptions of systems that keep changing or repeating. Studying them helps us ask what a mathematical object really is and whether changing an axiom changes only our language or also the objects we can work with. The topic also shows that one simple rule about sets can affect how we model streams, trees, and other repeating structures.

important_terms.definition: A set that can contain itself, or can belong to an endless chain of sets that contain one another.
A collection of things described using itself, such as saying that a group contains all finite groups made from that same group.
A rule in standard set theory that prevents sets from going around forever in membership chains.
A different rule that allows every suitable picture made from arrows to describe exactly one set.
An endless, ordered object with a first part called the head and a remaining part called the tail.

questions_to_think_about: Is a looping object always confusing, or can its pattern make it easier to understand?
Would you rather describe a stream as a pair with a tail or as an endless list? Why?
What might be useful about allowing a set to be part of itself?
Can two different pictures represent the same mathematical object?

summaries.example: Let s be a stream satisfying s = ⟨0,s⟩. Its first entry is 0, and removing its first entry gives s again. Intuitively, its unfolded form is the constant sequence (0,0,0, …). In ordinary set-theoretic coding, however, ordered pairs are themselves sets, so the literal equation creates an infinite descending membership pattern. The Foundation Axiom therefore rules out such an s as defined. Under AFA, the circular equation can receive a unique set-theoretic solution.
summaries.summary: The entry investigates circularity in set theory, concentrating on object circularity while also noting circular definitions. A non-wellfounded set may contain itself or participate in an infinite descending membership chain. Such objects are excluded in Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory by the Foundation Axiom, which corresponds to an iterative conception: sets arise in stages, and every set appears at some stage of the cumulative hierarchy. The entry studies replacing FA with the Anti-Foundation Axiom, first formulated in the relevant modern work by Forti and Honsell and developed influentially by Aczel. AFA states that every graph has a unique decoration. A decoration assigns a set to each node, with the value at a node determined by the values at its successors. Thus graphs and systems of set equations can represent circular sets, streams, and infinite trees. The stream equation s = ⟨0,s⟩ illustrates a central distinction. Its intuitive unfolding is an infinite sequence of zeros, and streams correspond bijectively with functions from the natural numbers to the natural numbers. Yet the stream-as-pair description and the function description can support different styles of reasoning. The entry then relates AFA to bisimulation, which matches successor structure in both directions, and to coalgebra. In this broader framework, AFA is associated with final coalgebras, greatest fixed points, coinduction, and corecursion, contrasting with initial algebras, least fixed points, induction, and recursion. The comparison is partly mathematical and partly a program for understanding bottom-up and top-down approaches.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes object circularity, involving an object’s membership structure, from definition circularity, involving a collection described using itself.
FA and AFA support contrasting conceptions of sets: iterative construction from earlier stages versus graph-based, coiterative structure.
AFA assigns a unique decoration to every graph, making circular set equations such as Ω = {Ω} solvable.
Streams can be represented directly as circular pairs or indirectly as functions from the natural numbers; the correspondence does not erase every conceptual difference.
Bisimulation identifies graph nodes with the same observable branching behavior and is central to the relation between graphs and hypersets.
Coalgebra organizes these ideas through final coalgebras, greatest fixed points, and corecursive definitions.
summaries.why_it_matters: The subject tests how much of set theory is about proving ordinary mathematical results and how much is about choosing a useful conception of mathematical objects. AFA can make circular structures directly available while preserving many familiar results when FA is not used. Even when circular objects can be represented indirectly in standard set theory, coalgebraic ideas may provide a clearer account of systems, observations, and repeating behavior. The topic therefore connects foundational philosophy with logic, semantics, and theoretical computer science without reducing those subjects to one another.

important_terms.definition: A set whose membership structure is not well-founded: for example, a set containing itself or lying on an infinite descending membership chain.
A set-theoretic principle stating that every graph has a unique decoration, or equivalently that suitable systems of set equations have unique solutions.
The standard principle excluding infinite descending membership chains and supporting the view that sets are built in stages.
The view that sets are generated step by step by iterating the power-set operation through the ordinals.
A view associated with AFA in which sets are assigned to nodes of graphs so that each node receives the set of values assigned to its successors.
A relation between graph nodes requiring matching successors in both directions; under AFA, bisimilar nodes receive the same set.
A mathematical framework studying systems through transitions and observations; it is presented as dual in important respects to algebraic, recursive approaches.
A method for defining or analyzing an object by repeatedly observing its structure, related to final coalgebras rather than initial algebras.

questions_to_think_about: If streams and functions correspond one-to-one, does that show they are the same objects, or only that they can play equivalent mathematical roles?
Does the fact that FA is optional for ordinary mathematics weaken the case for it, or merely show that its role is conceptual?
Why might a mathematician prefer a theory in which a circular equation has a unique solution?
How does bisimulation differ from simply checking whether two graph diagrams look alike?
What is gained by describing a theory through dual notions such as recursion/corecursion and induction/coinduction?

summaries.example: Think of a repeating playlist with three songs: A, then B, then C, and then back to A. We could write three linked stream rules: x begins with A and continues as y; y begins with B and continues as z; z begins with C and continues as x. The pattern unfolds as A, B, C, A, B, C, and so on. The entry asks whether the linked, looping streams should be treated as genuine objects, or only as ordinary infinite sequences.
summaries.summary: Non-wellfounded set theory examines what happens when mathematical objects are allowed to have circular membership structures. The entry first distinguishes two kinds of circularity. Object circularity concerns an object that is part of itself, perhaps through an endless chain. Definition circularity concerns describing a collection in terms of itself. Not every circular-looking equation is troublesome: some equations have a clear, unique solution, while others do not. Streams make the issue concrete. A stream has a head and a tail, and the tail can be another stream—or the original stream again. A short system of linked stream equations can therefore describe an endlessly repeating pattern. One can also unfold that pattern into an infinite sequence, understood in ordinary mathematics as a function from the natural numbers to the values. These two representations correspond, but the entry emphasizes that representation can affect how easily a definition is expressed. Standard set theory includes the Foundation Axiom. It rules out infinite descending membership chains and fits an iterative picture in which sets are formed in stages. Non-wellfounded set theory instead studies the Anti-Foundation Axiom. AFA says that every graph has a unique decoration: each point receives a set whose members are the values at the points reached by arrows. This makes circular sets, streams, and infinitely deep trees available as direct models. The entry connects this approach with coalgebra, which studies systems through transitions and observations. Its associated ideas—bisimulation, final coalgebras, coinduction, and corecursion—are presented as counterparts to more familiar algebraic and recursive ideas.
key_ideas: The entry separates circular objects from circular descriptions, since a self-referential description can sometimes be clarified by another definition.
Streams and infinite trees provide accessible models of circular structure.
In standard set theory, the Foundation Axiom supports the idea that sets are built in layers and blocks circular membership.
The Anti-Foundation Axiom allows graphs and set equations to represent circular structures with unique solutions.
A stream may be viewed as a loop-like pair or as an ordinary function listing its entries; both views correspond, but they encourage different reasoning.
Coalgebra supplies a wider language for circular systems, with ideas such as final coalgebras, coinduction, and corecursion.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic shows that axioms do more than provide technical rules: they can express different pictures of what mathematical objects are. The Foundation Axiom favors a bottom-up, stage-by-stage picture, while the Anti-Foundation Axiom supports a top-down or structural picture of circular systems. Comparing them helps explain why mathematicians might choose different representations for the same repeating pattern and why tools developed for set theory can also help describe systems in logic and computer science.

important_terms.definition: Circularity in which an object is part of itself, directly or through an endless chain of membership.
Circularity in which a collection or idea is described by referring back to that same collection or idea.
The usual set-theory rule that disallows endlessly descending chains of membership.
An alternative set-theory rule saying that every graph can be assigned a unique system of sets matching its arrows.
A drawing or structure made from points and arrows that can serve as a blueprint for sets.
A relation between two graph positions where each position’s possible next steps can be matched by the other’s.
A way of studying systems by focusing on their possible next states and observations.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a circular definition be harmless in one case but problematic in another?
Does an infinite sequence capture everything important about a looping stream?
What does the Foundation Axiom help us picture about how sets are formed?
Why would unique solutions be especially helpful when using graphs as blueprints?
Can two systems look different locally but still be equivalent under bisimulation?
